pages.body:
> 🧩 **Strand 4 — Computational Thinking**
Sub-strand 3: Robotics

It is time to build. In this unit you will learn Asimov’s laws of robotics, see how a robot is assembled, explore robot programming software and simulators, and construct a robot artefact from available components or in a simulator.

pages.title: Asimov’s Laws, Assembling a Robot and Robotics Software
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.4.3.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain Asimov’s three laws of robotics;
- demonstrate how a robot is assembled;
- explore robotics software packs; construct a robot artefact.
## Asimov’s three laws of robotics
The science-fiction writer **Isaac Asimov** introduced the **Three Laws of Robotics** in his 1942 short story “Runaround”. They are fiction, not real laws, but they are widely used to discuss **robot ethics** and safety.
| **Law** | **Statement (in summary)** |
|---|---|
| First Law | A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm. |
| Second Law | A robot must obey orders given by human beings, except where such orders would conflict with the First Law. |
| Third Law | A robot must protect its own existence, as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law. |
> 💡 **Think About It** Asimov later added a “Zeroth Law” about protecting humanity as a whole. Do self-driving cars, drones and AI systems need laws like these? Who should be responsible when a robot causes harm: the maker, the programmer or the owner?

pages.title: How a robot is assembled
pages.body:
## How a robot is assembled
1. **Plan the task:** e.g. a robot car that avoids obstacles.
2. **Build the chassis (body):** attach the motors and wheels to the base plate; add a caster wheel for balance.
3. **Mount the controller** (e.g. Arduino, micro:bit or mBot board) and the **motor driver**.
4. **Attach the sensors:** e.g. an ultrasonic distance sensor at the front, line sensors underneath.
5. **Wire** motors and sensors to the correct pins; add the **battery pack** and switch.
6. **Program** the controller on a computer and upload the code by USB or Bluetooth.
7. **Test and debug:** run the robot, observe, adjust code and mechanics, and repeat.
| **Robotics software / simulator** | **Description** |
|---|---|
| Scratch (with extensions) | Block coding with extensions for LEGO, micro:bit and other robots |
| mBlock (for mBot) | Scratch-based software for Makeblock mBot robots; also converts blocks to Python/Arduino code |
| LEGO MINDSTORMS EV3 / SPIKE | Kits with programmable bricks, motors and sensors; block or Python programming |
| Snap! | Block programming from UC Berkeley that can control some robots and devices |
| Webots | Free, open-source 3D robot **simulator**: program virtual robots without hardware |
| Lightbot and similar apps | Puzzle apps that teach robot programming logic |
| Tinkercad Circuits | Online simulator for Arduino circuits with motors and sensors |

pages.title: How a robot is assembled (continued)
pages.body:
> 💻 **Practical session — Construct a robot artefact**
**Option A (lab components):** In groups, build a simple robot using a kit (mBot, LEGO, micro:bit) or recycled materials with a small motor, battery and switch (e.g. a vibrating “bristlebot” or a motorised car). **Option B (simulator):** In Webots, Tinkercad or Scratch, program a virtual robot to move forward, detect an obstacle and turn. **For both:** draw your design, label the controller, sensors and actuators, write the algorithm (flowchart or pseudocode), test, improve and demonstrate your robot. Explain how it obeys Asimov’s laws.
> 🛡️ **Safety first** Use batteries of the correct voltage; never short-circuit battery terminals; keep fingers away from moving gears and wheels; use tools (screwdrivers, glue guns) under supervision.

> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. State Asimov’s three laws of robotics.
2. Outline **six** steps in assembling a robot car.
3. Compare building a physical robot with using a simulator: give **two** advantages of each.
